title: What is the Microkernel/Plugin architecture (stable core + plugins), and where does it fit (IDEs, CMS, rules engines)?
shortTitle: What is the Microkernel (Plugin) architecture, and where does it fit?
keyPoints: A minimal, stable core provides common functionality plus a registry and lifecycle for plugins.
Plugins implement a well-defined contract (interface) and add specific features without modifying the core.
Dynamic discovery via ServiceLoader or classpath scanning allows adding plugins without recompiling the core.
It fits systems that are fundamentally a stable engine plus many growing variations: IDEs, CMS, payment processors, rules engines.
The plugin contract is the most important design decision: a leaky or too-narrow contract forces core changes later.
Versioning the contract requires care (default methods for backward compatibility).
Third-party plugins may need sandboxing for security and isolation.

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a small stable core that defines a plugin contract and runs whatever plugins are registered, so new features arrive as new plugins without ever touching the core.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Core (microkernel)** – The minimal functionality needed to run the application plus the machinery to discover, register, and invoke plugins.
- **Plugins** – Independent components that each implement a well-defined plugin contract and provide one specific behavior.
- **Plugin contract** – An interface the core defines; the core never contains feature-specific logic, only the contract.
- **Dynamic discovery** – Java's `ServiceLoader`, classpath scanning, or runtime JAR loading lets plugins be added without recompiling.
- **Isolation** – A buggy plugin can be disabled without affecting others; sandboxing prevents one plugin from crashing the core.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the core banking engine at National Bank of India as a sturdy base that knows how to identify a customer, record a ledger entry, and run whatever product rule it is handed. By itself it offers no products. The actual products (home loan, car loan, credit card, fixed deposit) are plugins. Each follows the same standard contract. When the bank launches a new product, it writes a new plugin and drops it into the core's slot; the core is never rewritten.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The microkernel architecture splits a system into a minimal, stable core and a set of independent plugins. The core provides essential common functionality plus a registry and lifecycle for plugins, and importantly the plugin contract (an interface) that every plugin must implement. The core contains no feature-specific logic: it holds a registry, and when a request arrives, it asks each plugin whether it supports it and delegates to the matching one.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj designed the banking product engine this way. The core was a `ProductEngine` holding a registry of `ProductPlugin` instances, and each product (home loan, fixed deposit, car loan, credit card) was a plugin implementing the contract. Launching a new product meant writing a new plugin and registering it via ServiceLoader; the core was never touched and existing products were never at risk. When a pricing bug hit one product, Pankaj disabled just that plugin while the others kept serving.

The architecture fits anywhere the system is fundamentally a stable engine plus many growing variations: IDEs, browsers, CMS platforms, rules engines, and payment processors. The trade-offs are that designing the plugin contract is the hardest and most important decision because a leaky contract forces core changes later, versioning must be handled carefully with default methods for backward compatibility, and third-party plugins may need sandboxing for security.

Remember one sentence: Keep a small stable core that defines a plugin contract and a registry, and deliver every new feature as a new plugin so the system grows endlessly while the critical core stays untouched.
